Permanent Wounds are injuries that were not necessarily lethal but left the recipient permanently injured. They represent a serious impediment that requires creativity to overcome, especially at lower levels.

The effects of a Permanent Wound are irreversible unless the recipient is targeted with the __Regenerate__ spell, upon which one Permanent Wound is removed. Some of the effects of Permanent Wounds can be offset with Prosthetics or magical items.

table.title: Permanent Wounds
rows: Fatal Wound. Through an unrecoverable injury, you have been fatally wounded. You are now dead but can be brought back through normal methods.
Lost Arm[*]. A serious injury disables or destroys one of your arms. You can't use that arm to wield a weapon or a Shield, or to perform the Somatic component of a spell.

Lost Leg[*]. A serious injury disables or destroys one of your legs. Reduce your Speed by 15 feet, to a minimum of 5 feet. Your Speed can't be increased, and you can't take the Dash action. If you receive this result again your Speed is reduced by another 15 feet (to a minimum of 5 feet).

Lost Eye[*]. You lose an eye. You have Disadvantage on Wisdom (Perception) and Intelligence (Investigation) checks that rely on sight. If you receive this result again, you gain the Blinded condition.

Dizzy Spells. Undertaking vigorous activities leaves you addled. On odd numbered combat rounds, if you take an action, you cannot take a Bonus Action until the start of your next turn. If you take a Bonus Action, you cannot take an action until the start of your next turn.

Scarred Lungs. Your injury makes it a struggle to breathe. Your Hit Points maximum is permanently reduced by 1 for each of your character levels. Additionally, when you gain a level, your Hit Point maximum is reduced by 1.
Hideous Scar. You are horribly and visibly scarred. You have Disadvantage on Charisma (Performance) and Charisma (Persuasion) checks and Advantage on Charisma (Intimidation) checks.

Adrenaline Rush. Your injuries make you vulnerable to further damage, but your survival instincts are heightened in moments of danger. If you are Bloodied, any Critical Hit against you becomes a normal hit. If you are not Bloodied, attack rolls made against you score a Critical Hit on a roll of 19 or 20 on the d20.

Hesitant. Your psyche has been scarred more than your body. The first time after a Short, or Long Rest that you have to make a saving throw to avoid the Frightened condition, you are Frightened even if you succeed on the saving throw.
Old Pain. This lingering injury causes you intense pain when it flares up. When you roll a natural 1 on any D20 Test, you have the Incapacitated condition until the end of your next turn.

description.value: The rules in this section reviews two types of prophecies (greater prophecies and prophetic blessings/warnings), gives helpful suggestions on how to construct prophecies, and introduces a way to reward players for using prophecies. This section also includes a table of omens and a few predetermined sample prophecies.

description.name: Prophecies
description.value: Prophecies at their core are predictions of events to come. They often contain cryptic language that leaves them open to a myriad of interpretations. While prophecies might hint at destiny, they are open to interpretation because, by their very nature, they are vague. Unless handed down by a deity or powerful entity, the prophecies most Northerners encounter are communicated to them by seers. As mortal beings, seers can only grasp at the complex weavings of the __Norns__. This is why they speak in vague terms rather than in specific names, dates, and events. Prophecies given by seers are known as prophetic blessings or prophetic warnings.

*When the PCs receive omens or prophecies in a game, the strange sighting or cryptic words absolutely need to be open to different interpretation. They should be "signs" that can be interpreted differently depending on the person, hindsight, and circumstance. They can mean different things to different viewers, or even to the same viewer depending on how the campaign unfolds.*
*From a GM's perspective, the vagueness of an omen or prophecy keeps your options open in case the needs of the campaign change. It does the game no good if a specific prophecy is suddenly rendered useless when a PC dies unexpectedly. Instead of calling out the specific name of the trollkin druid PC, a good prophecy might refer to "Child of Two Worlds" or "Seeker of Balance." The new dwarven cleric PC in the game might fit those same titles. It's all a matter of interpretation. Flexibility is the power of prophecy for a GM. If the PCs hear a prophecy, but the events of the campaign end up different than the GM expected, the prophecy wasn't incorrect—the interpretation of it was.*
*More examples are included throughout this chapter, but here are a few helpful suggestions when creating omens or prophecies.*

entries: Couch prophecies in symbolism and mysteriously vague titles.
Make omens seem out of the ordinary but not immediately threatening.
Keep dates and locations vague or unclear.
Use kennings or allusions rather than the exact creature, site, or phenomenon you plan on using later.
Use metaphors or pseudonyms instead of specific names (especially the PCs' names).
Make sure prophecies can unfold in a few different ways.
Make sure omens can be seen in different ways.
Limit the scope of prophecies so they hint about a limited event not the entire scope of someone's life.
Use omens to foreshadow and/or enhance the mood you wish for the table.

description.name: Greater Prophecies
description.value: Greater prophecies are most commonly found in myths, legends, and tales, and they typically come directly from the __Norns__, detailing information for major life or world changes. These prophecies cryptically speak of fixed and unchangeable events in the future. Fantasy literature features this sort of prophecy often. In the Northlands, greater prophecies are exceedingly rare, as the __Norns__ don't often reveal the weft and weave of their loom to mere mortals. When PCs seek out a seer to hear a prophecy, they never receive greater prophecies. These are purely in the hands of the GM to give or withhold and should have a major impact on the story or world. They also typically don't have the benefits or consequences used in prophetic readings (detailed later in this section). The effects of fulfilling a greater prophecy are much larger than bonuses enjoyed by a single person, as these are outcomes that change nations.

description.name: Why Use Prophecies?
description.value: Prophecies can serve many functions in a campaign. They can be the focal point of the entire narrative, though this should be done sparingly, as the PCs, not a cryptic omen, should be driving the story. They can be used to provide information the GM wants to release in an in-game way. They can foreshadow future events, giving players a wonderful moment of "Oh! That's what the phrase 'Void Monarch' meant!" They can function as a through-line or guidepost for the campaign. When the players feel lost or out of focus, they can turn to the mysterious prophecy given by the GM to get the momentum of the campaign back on track. Finally, prophecies can be used as the fodder of the antagonist(s) in the campaign. The evil wizard might be searching for an ancient prophecy about a powerful relic, or the hoard of fanatical cultists might be invading because they follow the prophecy of their bloodthirsty deity. Above all else, remember that a prophecy is not fate.

description.name: Prophetic Readings (Blessings/Warnings) and Rewarding Fulfillment
description.value: Prophecies are broken up into prophetic blessings and warnings. In many games or stories, prophecies are traditionally relegated to the background, perhaps foreshadowing a coming event or giving the PCs a trail to follow. But they don't have to be. Prophetic blessings and warnings are brief glimpses of the loom of fate given to PCs by seers or supernatural creatures.

entries:
**Prophetic Blessing**: A prophecy suggesting an action during a certain sort of circumstance.
**Prophetic Warning**: A prophecy warning the PC to avoid a certain action during a certain sort of circumstance.

description.value: Each blessing or warning features three parts: a trigger, an action, and an outcome. The trigger is a short, cryptic element, circumstance, or description that the PC can recognize during game play. The action is an act or activity the PC takes in response to the trigger. The outcome is the result of the PC performing the action in response to the trigger. Outcomes are seen more often in greater prophecies but can also be used to add flavor to a prophecy. By design, the trigger, action, and outcome are vague and non-specific, allowing them to be applied to a wide variety of situations. When a PC (or GM) decides a trigger applies to something occurring in a game, they can act to fulfill the rest of the blessing or warning. Doing so gives the PC a magical benefit or lets them avoid a potential consequence.

entries: The PC approaches a seer and asks a specific question.
The player makes a prophecy roll to determine the power of the reading and if it is a blessing or a warning.
A blessing comes with a benefit and a warning comes with a consequence.
The benefit or consequence can be selected by the player, be the result of a roll on a random table, or be chosen by the GM.
The prophetic blessing or warning is generated using the tables shown later and contains at least one "trigger."
Later, the player or GM can decide if the trigger of their blessing or warning applies to a current circumstance in the game. If it does, they can attempt to fulfill it or avoid it.
For a prophetic blessing, the PC can perform the action described in the prophecy. If they do so, they gain the blessing's benefit.
For a prophetic warning, if the PC chooses to act in the way prohibited in the warning, they incur the warning's consequence.

description.name: Overview
description.value: The specifics of this system are detailed later, but in general here is how it works.

description.name: Creating a Prophecy
description.value: This section demonstrates how to create greater prophecies and prophetic blessings or warnings. If you are creating a greater prophecy, you can skip to Step 3: Generate the Prophecy.

description.name: Step 1: Prophecy Roll
description.value: The first step in creating a prophetic blessing or warning is the prophecy roll. When a seer or other entity gives a prophetic blessing or warning to a PC, the player must roll a prophecy roll to determine the power of the reading and whether it is a prophetic blessing or a warning. This roll is a simple d20 roll plus the PC's reputation modifier (see Reputation), or half of the PC's Proficiency Bonus, whichever is higher.
[See Prophecy Roll Table's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#prophecy%20roll%20table_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Step 2: Determining Benefits and Consequences
description.value: The next step is to determine any consequences or benefits of a prophetic reading. Players can choose a benefit with their GMs approval, they can roll a d8 and consult the appropriate table, or the GM can choose it for them. Consequences are best chosen by the GM or determined randomly.

Each blessing/warning grants a game-specific aspect to the PC when the prophetic reading is fulfilled. Benefits and consequences are divided into three levels: Least, Greater, and Legendary/Dire. The relative power of the benefit or consequence increases with each stage.

Each benefit and consequence lists its duration. If a duration seems not to fit the listed benefit or consequence due to the specific circumstances of the game, the GM can change the duration. A GM can always choose to extend or end an effect, if doing so would better support the prophecy.
[See Legendary Benefits and Dire Consequences's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#legendary%20benefits%20and%20dire%20consequences_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Step 3: Generating the Prophecy
description.value: The third step in the process features tables allowing GMs to select (or roll randomly to determine) the triggers, actions, and, optionally, the outcomes of the prophetic readings. GMs can also use the tables to generate a greater prophecy.
Prophecies (especially prophetic blessings or warnings) typically begin with either "When" or "If," and the trigger and action together should form a complete sentence.

description.name: Trigger
description.value: To determine the trigger, roll a d20 once for each column in the Trigger table, combining the outcome into a vague description. GMs can use a bit of poetic license to make the trigger sound better. For example, if the rolls determined the words "Dry/Wet," "Guardian," "Bellows," and "Holy Place," the resulting trigger might be "When the arid guardian bellows in the holy temple."
[See Trigger Table's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#trigger%20table_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Action
description.value: To create the action, roll a d20 for each column in Action table and combine the outcome into a vague description. Due to the number of possible results, GMs should rearrange the results and/or add words as necessary so the action makes sense. For example, if the rolls determined the words "Run," "Relic," "Behind," and "Concealment," the resulting trigger might be rephrased as "Run from behind the concealed relic," with the word "from" added for clarity.

If the prediction is a prophetic warning, the action element must be described as something to avoid. Remember, the GM will be the one identifying a trigger as being active, but they might not share that information with the players. For example, if your rolls determined a different set of words, such as "Hold," "Relic," "Inside," and "Light," the prophetic warning might be "Don't hold the relic inside the light."
[See Action Table's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#action%20table_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Outcomes
description.value: An outcome is a change to the world, for good or for ill. The Outcome tables below offer suggestions for changes, both large and small, that could occur when a greater prophecy is fulfilled. Prophetic blessings and warnings don't usually have an outcome because the benefit or consequence serves that role. If GMs wish to use an outcome with a prophetic reading, they should begin each outcome with the word "to," such as "To derive new knowledge..." Outcomes should be matched with the nature of the benefit or consequence. For example, the "gods bestowing a blessing" could be used for attacks having Disadvantage against you.

To create an outcome, choose a column in the table (or roll a d4 to determine it randomly) and then roll a d20 for that column. Reword the outcomes as needed to fit the prophecy's trigger and action and to form a complete sentence. Typically, prophecies only have one outcome, but GMs can certainly add a second for particularly momentous predications. Greater prophecies always have an outcome attached to them.

When presenting an outcome in a prophecy, the outcome should be phrased as an event that has not happened, yet also in a manner to fit with the "When" or "If" that began the prediction. Use words like "will," "shall," and "lest" to indicate a future tense.
For example, rolling a d4 and a d20 to choose a random outcome results in "Sleeping god awakens" (a societal change), giving us a prophecy that, if triggered, will cause a sleeping god to wake up.
[See Outcome Table's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#outcome%20table_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Final Prophecy
description.value: After going through these steps, the trigger, action, and benefit/consequence (or outcome) should form a complete sentence. Using the samples we've seen so far, a prophetic reading with a greater blessing would be: "When the arid destroyer bellows in the holy temple, run from behind the concealed relic to gain __Volund__'s protection." (Resistance to fire damage) Using the samples, a greater prophecy would be: "When the arid destroyer bellows in the holy temple, run from behind the concealed relic, and the sleeping god will awaken."

description.name: Sample Prophetic Blessings and Warnings
description.value: Presented here are several prophetic blessings and warnings along with possible interpretations to show how players can identify the triggers in different ways. Some elements of these samples are not found in the tables in Step 3, to demonstrate how GMs can invent their own.

description.name: Least Prophetic Blessing
description.value: *When the storm casts its shadow, seek shelter within the ancient to sip from Mimir's well.*
**Benefit**: If you do so, you gain Advantage on Intelligence- and Wisdom-based ability checks for 1 hour.

entries: Shadow of the storm could be a literal storm overhead. But it could also be a creature or situation. The fury of a giant could be described as a "storm," so then the giant's shadow might be identified as the trigger.

A player could "seek shelter within the ancient" by moving into an old structure. But "ancient" could also be a term for a mountain, so stepping into a cave would fulfill the action portion of the blessing. Similarly, moving beneath the branches of a mighty tree could be viewed as seeking shelter within the ancient.

description.name: Legendary Prophetic Blessing
description.value: *When the stars hide their faces, quench the wound-brand to strike like Sleipnir.*

**Benefit**: If you do so, once in the next 24 hours, you can use an action to move up to twice your speed and make a melee attack. You don't provoke Opportunity Attacks when moving in this way. If you successfully hit a creature, the target is pushed 10 feet away from you and has the prone condition.

entries: Stars hiding their faces could be a kenning for darkness. It could also be interpreted more literally as people looking away from a situation.

The most obvious meaning for "quenching the wound-brand" would be to take something on fire and extinguish it. But wound-brand could be a kenning for a sword or weapon, and quenching is a smithing term for plunging hot metal into water. So instead, a player might take that to mean they merely have to stick their weapon into water.

description.name: Greater Prophetic Warning
description.value: *When the light speaks in screams, don't answer the call with wyrd-craft, or suffer Thor's fate.*

**Consequence**: If you cast a spell before the end of your next turn, you have the Poisoned condition for 1d4 rounds. While you have the Poisoned condition from this effect, your thoughts are muddled, so you can only cast cantrips.

entries: The light speaking in screams could be something like a __Fireball__, which is bright and causes screams of pain. It could also be a glowing foe who is yelling.

The warning against answering the call with wyrd-craft is pretty straightforward as it is referring to spellcasting. That said, a player could instead decide wyrd-craft refers to an enchanted weapon, thus the warning would say not to attack the "screaming light."

description.name: Dire Prophetic Warning
description.value: *When an ancient roar fractures the land, don't spill the dew of slaughter, or your hand will betray your allies.*

**Consequence**: The first time you deal damage with an attack at any point in the next 8 hours, you become cursed for 1 minute. While cursed, at the start of each of your turns, roll a d6. On a result of 1 or 2, you must move and make a melee attack against a random creature. If you can't reach a creature with your movement, you can instead take the Dash action to move toward a random creature.

entries: An ancient roar fracturing the land could be an earthquake, but it could just as easily be a yelling giant striking the ground with her club, or an erupting volcano.

The warning not to spill the dew could be viewed as meaning "don't spill a container or vessel nearby." The phrase "dew of slaughter" is a kenning for blood, so it could also be a warning not to spill blood, either your own or (more likely in this case) the blood of a foe.

description.name: Sample Greater Prophecies
description.value: Here is a complex Greater Prophecy crafted using the various tables described in this section. As shown here, GMs can roll several times on the various tables to make longer prophecies if they wish.

description.name: Sample Greater Prophecy
description.value: "When a great king withholds secrets, and the statue of the brave awakens in the village square, bind well the rune-carved blade with blessed steel, or the forbidden rite shall unearth the sleeping god. Should this come to pass, hope can yet be restored if the fractured binding is cast anew with bloody stone."

description.name: Construction
description.value: This complicated greater prophecy follows this format, with some additional words thrown in for clarity:

entries: Trigger (great king withholds secrets)
Trigger (statue awakes in village)
Action (bind blade with steel)
Outcome (forbidden rite awakens a god)
Outcome (hope is restored)
Trigger (fractured binding cast anew)
Action (with bloody stone)

description.name: Omens
description.value: Small signs, portents, and sightings work hand-in-hand with prophecies to foreshadow future events. While not as informative as a prophecy, omens provide flavor and can increase the mystery and tension in a game. GMs can use them as much or as little as they wish, but a good balance is different for every game, campaign, and table. Include too many omens and the GM risks blunting their impact. Provide too few omens and the table won't have the tone or vibe the GM is striving for.

The tables in this section provide examples of three different types of omens to add into a game: hopeful, foreboding, and mysterious. Some are portents of good things, others are warnings of dire events, and some are just mysterious. GMs can use these suggestions as a base and invent their own omens.

In most cases, the GM should choose the type of omen they wish, altering the omen as needed to fit the circumstances of the campaign, but if a more random generation method is preferred, roll a d4 and consult the Omen Types table.
[See Omen Types's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#omen%20types_northlandsworldbook)
[See Hopeful Omens's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#hopeful%20omens_northlandsworldbook)
[See Foreboding Omens's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#foreboding%20omens_northlandsworldbook)
[See Mysterious Omens's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#mysterious%20omens_northlandsworldbook)

In the culture of the Northlands, raiding other communities dates back to the Reaving. These expeditions served a variety of purposes depending on who conducted them. For some, they were a method of earning glory, training young warriors, punishing foes, or (more typically) securing badly needed resources. Historically, raids involved securing a ship, gathering a crew, sailing often great distances to a location, attacking it, and returning with treasure. Played out fully, a raid could be a campaign all by itself, and GMs are certainly free to run them that way. These optional rules, however, allow various portions of the raiding journey, or even the entire raid, to occur "off-stage" by abstracting them. This keeps raids feeling fast and thrilling.

description.name: A Word About Theft and Raiding
description.value: For a Northlander, raiding is not the same as thievery. To steal something from someone is not honorable and violates the various rules of hospitality. Raiding, however, is not "theft" because you are fighting someone for their treasures. Even if the "battle" consists of sneaking up on a location, setting it on fire, and cutting down the inhabitants as they flee the blaze, it's considered a fight and thus an honorable means to seize the rewards. The general guideline for a reaver is anything goes, as long as it doesn't stain their honor.

The typical goal of a raid isn't to take territory or inflict the most damage. Instead, it is to gather the most resources or treasure without losing too many warriors or your own supplies in the process. Thus, raids tended to be lightning-fast assaults rather than sieges.

description.name: Using Raiding Rules
description.value: These rules break raids down into abstract phases—preparation, journey, raid, and return—with each phase determined by rolling dice and consulting tables. Successes or failures from each phase affect the next subsequent phase. A few other aspects are also abstracted for ease of play.

In general, 1 spoil is worth 500 GP, regardless of it being a bag of grain, bars of steel, a pouch of gems, or a crate of chickens. This isn't a replacement for standard treasure; instead, it serves as a shorthand for the "wealth" taken during the raid. The spoils gained in a raid reflect what goes directly to the PCs. This assumes NPCs already received a separate share of the proceeds of the successful raid.

The abstractions presented by this system provide a way for PCs to track the costs and rewards of a raid without getting bogged down in the minutia of weights and cargo lists. However, any phase can be replaced with actual in-game play according to the needs of the GM. For example, the preparation, journey, and return phases could be handled abstractly, but the raid itself could be a full combat encounter.
[See Raiding Targets (Abstracted)'s stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#raiding%20targets%20(abstracted)_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Cost
description.value: To participate in the raid, a PC must spend coins, as determined by the target of the raid (see the [Raiding Target](https://5e.tools/tables.html#raiding%20target_northlandsworldbook) tables). This is an abstracted cost reflecting a share of the cost of outfitting the expedition, but in return, the PC gets a greater share of plunder taken.

description.name: Time
description.value: Raiding activities are typically measured in weeks, each of which is roughly assumed to be at least 5 days, where 8 hours per day are spent pursuing the current activity. Each phase of the raid indicates the amount of time in "weeks" that occurred.

description.name: Distance
description.value: While it is important for the GM to know how far the target of the raid is, the exact distance is somewhat meaningless for the purposes of these rules. More distant targets chosen during the preparation phase may require GMs to adjust the tables in other phases to account for the particulars of various climates, hazards, flora, and fauna found in those locations.

description.name: Raiding Roll and Spoils Dice
description.value: Just as the time and distance of the raid are handled abstractly, the actual raid and the amount of plunder taken is abstracted in a mechanic similar to rolling attack and weapon damage in combat. While raiding, PCs make a raiding roll against a DC determined by the size of the target (plus any additional modifiers). If successful, the PCs then roll a spoils die to determine how much plunder is gained.

description.name: Raiding Phases
description.value: The four phases of a raid are preparation, journey, raid, and return, and they are detailed here.

*Not all raids need to be conducted via the sea. The communities of giants to the North offer tantalizing targets for metal, rare resources, hides, and relics. Due to the geography of the Northlands, most reavers utilize ships for direct assaults on raiding targets or to travel to a landing site near the target for an overland attack. Raiding PCs aren't required to use ships if their target is reachable by marching, though most groups of warriors won't want to trek hundreds of miles across frozen mountains when they could just sail there.*

*Are the PCs leading the raid themselves? Or are they joining a raid led by an NPC? Either way, the players are the ones making decisions for the raid and will exert a degree of narrative control over all of the NPCs involved in it. If the PCs join a raid led by an NPC, the cost they pay up front is a bit like investing in the expedition. If it is successful, the PCs get a larger share of the plunder than the average warrior. GMs can, of course, have NPC leaders push for larger shares, perhaps setting up some fun roleplaying confrontations.*

*The raiding rules presented in this chapter can be used as downtime activities. Typically, this works best if all of the PCs choose to embark on the raid together, especially since most raids take at least two weeks to conduct. GMs can shorten this time by giving the raid expedition a few of the ship upgrades or special resources that reduce the sailing time. This might be advisable if some of the PCs go raiding and others stay behind. That way, everyone is on the same time frame.*

description.name: Preparation
description.value: In the first phase, the PCs determine the following aspects.

entries: **The Target**: Choose the place to be raided.
**Ship Upgrades**: Pay for additional upgrades for the ship.
**Additional Raiders**: Recruit a crew of hearty warriors.
**Special Resources**: Gather provisions, ship repair materials, and deal with other details for the journey.
**The Cost**: After calculating the total based on their choices, PCs each pay a share to fund the raid.

description.value: Making wise choices during the preparation phase can mean the difference between a successful raid and an abject failure.

description.name: Journey
description.value: In the second phase, the PCs must contend with the voyage to the raiding target, overcoming hazards and obstacles. Success or failure when doing so can grant bonuses (or penalties) during the next phase.

description.name: Raid
description.value: In the third phase, the raiders reach their destination and conduct a fast assault on the target before additional defenders can be mobilized to oppose them. The PCs make a raiding roll and roll the spoils die to determine the level of the raid's success and the amount of plunder taken. How things go here can directly impact the ease (or difficulty) of their trip home.

description.name: Return
description.value: In the fourth phase, the PCs return home, hopefully with their ship laden with spoils. Much like the journey phase, the return features hazards and obstacles. This phase can be more difficult if the raid went poorly.

description.name: Outcome
description.value: Once all of the phases are complete, the GM tallies up the positive and negative results of the entire voyage to determine the final spoils of the raid.

description.name: Preparation Phase
description.value: The preparation phase involves recruiting warriors, upgrading a ship, and gathering supplies for the raid. But the first decision to be made is to choose a target.

description.name: The Target
description.value: Raids can be carried out on various targets, from small hamlets, to forts, to major cities. The dangers the reavers might face, including armed defenders, increase with the scale of the target, but so do the possible rewards.
The PCs can use the Raiding Targets table to choose the target of their raid, as well as the types of loot typically found in the listed communities.

If the GM plans to run the raid phase as an encounter, a table of different settlement sizes has been provided to show the average number of defenders. The number of reavers needed to raid various settlements detailed in the abstracted table is the same here.
[See Raiding Targets (As an Encounter)'s stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#raiding%20targets%20(as%20an%20encounter)_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Ship Upgrades
description.value: The choice of ship, number of warriors, supplies, and so forth are abstracted in this system. The funds paid by the PCs to participate in the raid include an appropriately sized ship crewed by enough warriors to attempt the raid against the chosen target settlement.

If the players and GM wish to explore ship options in more detail, consult the Naval Combat section earlier in this chapter. Additionally, Chapter 5 contains specific information about the most common vessels used in the North. As a reminder, all crew members are expected to operate the vessel as well as participate in the raid itself.

As part of the preparation phase, the PCs can choose to enhance their ship with a variety of options. Each of these enhancements gives the PCs a bonus to their raiding roll, spoil dice, or other mechanics, but using them also increases the cost each PC must pay to participate in the raid. Each upgrade is only usable once during this raid to give a bonus in one phase. If an upgrade is not used, it is wasted. These upgrades don't have any mechanical function in naval combat.
[See Ship Upgrades's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#ship%20upgrades_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Additional Raiders
description.value: A contingent of warriors large enough to tackle the chosen target comes with the funds paid by the PCs. However, some parties might wish to bring more warriors along to ensure victory. The PCs are not going to be able to empty a village of warriors to crew their longship. At best, they'll convince half of a community's able-bodied reavers to sign on. Raiding is a risk not only for those participating but also for the communities they leave behind. Every raider lost during a raid means one fewer warrior to defend the village against monsters or raids, as well as one fewer worker to do the vital tasks to keep the settlement going.
In general, the size of community hosting the raid (or the place where the raid leaves from) directly relates to the number of extra warriors available to be recruited.

Additional warriors can be hired in bands, ranging from 5 to 100. Each group gives a bonus to the raiding roll during the raid phase, but it also comes with an associated cost added to the sum the PCs pay to fund the raid (see the Extra Warriors table). Only one group of extra warriors can be added to each raid.
[See Extra Warriors's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#extra%20warriors_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Special Resources
description.value: The base level funds provided by the PCs provide a decent amount of provisions, repair materials, and other supplies for the raid. Aside from that, there are special resources PCs can purchase (see the Special Resources table). Similar to ship upgrades, these resources give bonuses to raiding rolls, spoils dice, and other game elements. Each special resource is only usable once during a raid to give a bonus in one phase. If a special resource is not used, it is wasted.
[See Special Resources's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#special%20resources_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: The Journey
description.value: In the second phase, the PCs must contend with the voyage to the raiding target while overcoming hazards and obstacles. Success or failure can grant bonuses (or penalties) during the next phase. The PCs make a group roll on the Sea/Land Journey table for each week of travel (see Abstracted Time/Distance in this section). GMs can choose to add additional rolls on the Sea/Land Journey table as they wish. To emphasize the epic themes of the raid, the GM should be as descriptive as possible.

description.name: Abstracted Time/Distance
description.value: Rather than delve into the minutia of travel speeds and distance, those aspects are abstracted in the journey phase to 1 week of time for most destinations. The GM can always add time to the voyage to account for things such as setting elements or for more distant destinations.
[See Sea/Land Journey Table's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#sea%2Fland%20journey%20table_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: The Raid
description.value: In the third phase, the PCs reach their destination and conduct a fast assault on the target before additional defenders can be mobilized to oppose them.

description.name: Raiding Roll
description.value: The moment has come! Screaming their battle cries, the reavers leap from their longboats or charge through the snow-covered field toward the (hopefully) unsuspecting settlement. Determining the result of a raid requires the players to make a group raiding roll against the DC of the target settlement.

The raiding roll is equal to 1d20, modified by any bonuses or penalties gained during the previous phases. If the result of this roll meets or exceeds the DC, the raid succeeds and grants a bonus to the spoils die, as well as additional benefits. However, a result lower than the DC indicates the raiders were driven off but still managed to grab some plunder on the way out. Rolling below the DC gives a penalty to the spoils die and may result in other complications. The Raiding Roll table displays all of these results.
[See Raiding Roll's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#raiding%20roll_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Important NPC Captives
description.value: If the raid captures an important NPC, that individual can be ransomed back to their family or community. The negotiations and exchange can take some time, but many Northlands jarls are more than pleased to take such captives off the PCs hands in exchange for favors, like gaining renown or learning hidden lore, or for a lump sum of gold, a magic item, or another reward determined by the GM.

description.name: Spoils Die
description.value: Once the raiding roll is resolved, the PCs can roll the spoils die for the target settlement, adding any adjustments incurred during the current and previous phases. As a reminder, the result of this roll is the share of plunder going directly to the PCs. The raiding rules assume NPC warriors receive a separate share from the total among of loot taken.

description.name: The Return
description.value: In the fourth phase, the PCs travel home (hopefully) laden with spoils from a successful raid. Repeat the journey phase, adjusting rolls as necessary. This phase can be more difficult if the raid went poorly, and failures here can cost the PCs a portion of their spoils.

description.name: Outcome
description.value: Once all of the phases are complete, the GM and the players tally up the positive and negative results of the entire voyage to determine the final spoils of the raid.
The total spoils handed to the PCs can be immediately exchanged for gold pieces or standard equipment of equal value. One spoil is worth 500 GP.

With GM approval, PCs can instead exchange their spoils for magic items. The availability of items depends on the size of the settlement the PCs return to after their raid is complete. Typically, this is the same location they left from, but that isn't a requirement. The Spoils Exchange table shows the number of spoils that can be exchanged for magic items of different rarities, as well as the minimum size of the settlement likely to have such an item.

The exact nature of an item gained by the PCs should be a discussion between the players and the GM. Since magic item rarity offers a wide range of value for items, not every item will be available just because they have enough spoils to exchange for it. Settlements might also charge more for certain items than is shown on the table, due to campaign circumstances. The GM makes the final determination on all magic item availability and cost.
[See Spoils Exchange's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#spoils%20exchange_northlandsworldbook)

This house rule lets characters grab and drink a potion as a bonus action, enabling them to heal or buff up in combat without sacrificing their primary attacks or spellcasting to do so. (This applies to enemies and NPCs as well as player characters!)

Using this house rule, you can use a bonus action to drink a potion yourself. It still requires an action to administer a potion to another creature. You can also choose to only apply this house rule to potions of healing and their variants (potion of greater healing, etc.). In this less powerful version of the house rule, you can consume a potion that restores hit points as a bonus action, but all other potions still require you to use your action.

Whenever a d20 must be rolled, roll three Success Dice instead and add them together. If the roll has disadvantage, all the Success Dice that come up showing a result in an outlined number (1, 2, or 3) are considered to have given a result of zero instead. If the roll has advantage, roll four Success Dice instead of three and add them together.

An individual's reputation is of paramount importance to the people of the North. As canny __Wotan__ said, "Cattle die, kin die, even the self dies, but glory never dies for the one able to achieve it." To be a hero in the Northlands, and thus earn a place in the afterlife, is to perform deeds with an eye toward how they shape your reputation. Yet, renown isn't static—it ebbs and flows. A hero might gain great honor for killing a mighty dragon, but if they act dishonorably, their reputation will tarnish and rot away.

Reputation is an optional rule that tracks your character's prestige and provides a way to leverage that renown to perform cinematic and epic actions by temporarily assuming narrative control of the game.

description.name: Character Reputation Score
description.value: Your character's reputation is measured by a score much like an ability score modifier. A novice warrior might have +1 reputation, while the greatest champion of the realm might have +10 or higher. Unlike ability scores, this modifier begins at 0 and is not adjusted due to skills or characters levels. Reputation increases when you perform gain renown for deeds and noteworthy acts of daring, and it decreases if you are caught committing dishonorable acts. Multiple characters can gain reputation by performing the same deed together. The [Reputation Thresholds](https://5e.tools/tables.html#reputation%20thresholds_northlandsworldbook) table shows the levels and benefits of reputation.

Note, this system specifically governs what people know about you. If no one witnesses you committing a dishonorable act, your reputation in the mortal world won't suffer. Similarly, if you slay a great wyrm, but no one believes you, your reputation won't improve. Gods, __Norns__, and other divine beings might be aware of what you did, and it might affect your chances of going to Valhalla, but unless other people witness or learn of what you did, your reputation modifier will not change.

description.name: Deeds and Dishonorable Acts
description.value: Deeds are acts of heroism accomplished by the PC or party, like saving a village from raiders, slaying a dragon, or finding a fabled lost treasure. Acts need not be victorious combat to count as deeds. A merchant who brings back a longship laden with goods can gain renown, as can an artist who creates a masterpiece. As your character accomplishes deeds, they gain more reputation, advancing through various thresholds or stages, but they can lose reputation by getting caught acting dishonorably. You should keep track of the number of deeds you have accomplished, as they determine your reputation threshold.

It is important to note that a deed isn't every amazing thing an adventurer does. Deeds need to be notable, worthy of saga and song. As a general guideline, a deed is something a PC or party does that dramatically alters the storyline of the game. So fighting monsters is not necessarily a deed since almost everyone in the Northlands does that frequently, but driving away the legendary ice worm might be. If you accomplish the same deed twice, the second usually doesn't count as a deed. The GM and the player should decide together what accomplishments count as a deed.

description.name: Rule of Five
description.value: If you accomplish five deeds, and others learn of them, you advance to the next threshold level.

description.name: Dishonorable Acts
description.value: The antithesis of deeds are dishonorable acts. Violence isn't necessarily dishonorable nor is killing. In the North, major dishonorable acts include murdering an innocent, breaking an oath, breaking the rules of hospitality, violating the peace of the althing, and cowardice in the face of danger. The GM should determine if your actions are dishonorable acts and if enough people have found out about them to damage your reputation.

description.name: Rule of Three
description.value: If you commit three dishonorable acts that others learn about, you lose all accumulated deeds and are reduced by one threshold level.

description.name: Thresholds
description.value: Thresholds are best described as "reputation levels" measuring your character's renown. Each stage has prerequisites based on character level and provides small regional bonuses.

At each stage, you must accomplish five deeds to advance to the next threshold, however, you can't move to the next threshold until you reach the character level minimum of that threshold. For example, a level 3 character with 5 deeds can't gain more reputation or move from the Obscure to the Known reputation threshold until they reach level 5. Each time you advance to a new threshold, your deeds counter resets to 0.

Your threshold level also determines what type of reputation challenge you can attempt and a few minor benefits. You must be in an area where your reputation is known (as determined by the GM) to benefit from the regional bonuses.
[See Reputation Thresholds's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#reputation%20thresholds_northlandsworldbook)
[See Threshold Regional Benefits's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#threshold%20regional%20benefits_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Reputation Challenges
description.value: Once per character level, you can leverage your fame and renown to attempt a Reputation Challenge. If you succeed, you take narrative control of the game for a limited time, essentially becoming the GM to resolve the dramatic moment. If you fail, you lose reputation as the word of your failure spreads. This places a tremendous amount of power in your hands, and as such, the GM can always step in if things get out of hand.

description.name: Making a Challenge
description.value: As a Reaction at any time, you can announce you are making a Reputation Challenge. With GM agreement, you can even do so if you have already used a Reaction this turn.

When you make a Reputation Challenge, you must explain to the GM what your PC plans to do. Be descriptive and dramatic as this moment should be a heroic! The GM might suggest alterations but generally should work with you to agree on what happens to your character, the other PCs, and the world of the game. This is called the "narrative."

entries: **Challenge Types**: As part of the narrative, you must also decide what challenge type you are attempting: Low, Medium, High, or Epic. You must meet the reputation threshold prerequisite to attempt any challenge. The GM might rule your proposed narrative sounds like a higher type than you qualify for, so you might have to scale things back.

**Low Challenge (DC 10)**: This represents a heroic action or dramatic moment that influences the immediate situation or a small group of people. It might turn the tide of a small battle, impress a local lord, or rally a frightened village.

**Medium Challenge (DC 12)**: This represents a major feat that affects an entire town, settlement, or faction's immediate course of action. It can reshape relationships, affect regional politics, or change the direction of a local conflict.
**High Challenge (DC 14)**: This reshapes the destiny of an entire region, kingdom, or major power. It brings about permanent shifts in the world's politics, military balances, or magical forces.
**Epic Challenge (DC 16)**: This represents mythic-level events that echo across nations, planes, and generations. These deeds are worthy of legend and saga and may change the course of the world.

description.name: Challenge Roll
description.value: After you and the GM agree on the narrative and challenge type, you must roll a d20 plus your reputation bonus to determine the outcome.

description.name: Success
description.value: If you succeed, your proposed narrative happens as you described it.

description.name: Failure
description.value: If you fail the challenge roll, you lose all of your accumulated deeds and are reduced by one reputation threshold.

description.name: Challenge Guidelines
description.value: Taking control of the game is intended to give you a narrative way for your characters to overcome obstacles and be the dynamic heroes you've imagined them to be. It is NOT a method to one-shot a bad guy or to suddenly gain personal wealth. While this feature gives you control of the narrative for a moment, don't forget that your character's story is also part of the world and part of the rest of the party's story. Be polite, be respectful, include others, and have fun!
Here are some general guidelines for your narratives:

entries: Your narrative can happen during combat or outside it.

The amount of time your narrative takes is enough to complete the description of the challenge you discussed with the GM. As indeterminate as it sounds, the time of this can vary. Low challenges might only be a couple of rounds, while an Epic challenge might take an hour, a day, or even more.
What you describe should be within the bounds of logic, even if it's rather unlikely.
In general, you don't need to roll for narrative actions, though the GM may add new obstacles into your narrative that require a roll.
Your narrative takes the same amount of time as your normal turn, or longer if the GM allows.

Your narrative can include multiple actions, but unless the GM allows it, you can't cast more than one spell or make more than your normal number of attacks, unless you could otherwise cast more than one in a turn or make more than your normal number of attacks in a turn, such as through a Fighter's Action Surge feature.

If you attack a foe with weapons or spells, you can choose to roll normally, or with your GM's approval, you can automatically hit and kill a number of foes equal to half your Proficiency Bonus if each creature's CR is equal to or less than half your character's level.
You can add or change elements of the world to fit your narrative, if the changes are logical and approved by the GM.
Don't interfere with other players' agency for their characters, and/or be sure to consult with other players if their characters have a role to play in your narrative.

description.value: *The Lord of the Rings Roleplaying* employs a variant of the standard 5e rules for short and long rests.

entries: Player-heroes can benefit from long rests exclusively in sheltered and safe refuges (i.e. not 'on the road'). The safe havens of the Company certainly count as sheltered refuges, as well as any city or settlement where the Company is welcomed on friendly terms. At the Loremaster's discretion, a deserted but well-sheltered place in the wilds could also be suitable for a long rest.

Additionally, a short rest during a journey must be at least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps or performs only light activities. Once the Player-heroes stop travelling for at least 24 hours (because they have reached their destination, or have decided to stop along the way), they can resume taking short rests of 1 hour.

description.value: Virtues are unique abilities and special talents, characteristic of a given culture. Players select a new virtue when their Player-hero reaches certain levels in a calling.
Rewards are pieces of war gear of superior craftsmanship, granted to a Player-hero as an award for their deeds when they reach certain levels. Rewards are not tied to a specific culture.
Virtues and rewards are described Chapter 4.

During combat, if the attack roll shows two or more icons, the attack hits regardless of any modifier or the target's AC, and is a critical hit. If the roll has disadvantage, it must show three icons.
If the Success Dice for an attack only show outlined numbers, the attack misses regardless of any modifiers or the target's AC.

Challenging an almost all-powerful Enemy and facing its terrible minions is bound to instil a sense of fear and doubt in the Player-heroes, a sentiment that in time comes to weigh heavily on their hearts and minds. In *The Lord of the Rings Roleplaying*, this burden is represented by the accumulation of Shadow points, and by the sources that force their gain.

entries: Player-heroes can resist some sources of Shadow gain by making a saving throw—either an Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma saving throw.
Attempting or performing misdeeds provokes an automatic Shadow gain instead, as such actions prove that a hero is falling for the evil ways of the Enemy.

description.value: Player-heroes mark their descent into the Shadow following a specific Shadow path, based on their chosen calling, and risk leaving the game if they cannot stop their descent into madness. Player-heroes avoid this by getting rid of Shadow points during the Fellowship Phase, resting from actively opposing the Enemy.
*Shadow can also result in the Player-heroes being subjected to two new conditions, anguished and miserable.*
These conditions, along with the rules for the Shadow, are presented in Chapter 8.
The naval combat rules presented here are intended to make the ship a dynamic and exciting part of any conflict.

description.name: Ship Siege Weapons
description.value: In the real-world cultures that inspired the Northlands, longships typically didn't utilize ship-mounted siege weapons. Instead, the warriors aboard them made use of melee and ranged weapons they could carry, not relying on weaponized machinery to do their battles. Depending on your setting of choice, weapons such as ballistae or mangonels may be loaded onto a longship if it suits your style of play. For such times, siege weapons are included in longship entries in Chapter 5, which can be removed if they do not make sense for your particular game.

Ship-mounted weapon attack rolls are equal to the Strength or Dexterity modifier of the ship (whichever is higher). The damage bonus is also equal to the higher of the ships Strength or Dexterity modifier. A PC firing a ship-mounted weapon can choose to use their own ranged weapon attack bonus and damage bonus instead of the ship's if they wish, using the higher of their Strength or Dexterity.

entries:
**Ballista**: A massive crossbow that fires weighted bolts. A ship-mounted ballista can be loaded and aimed by the crew using the Operate Ship Weapon action.
**Naval Ram**: This metal and wood ram is mounted to the front of the ship at or below the water level. It can be used to smash a hole in the side of another vessel. If the ship moves more than 30 feet first, a ram deals an additional 1d10 Piercing damage.
**Ship Catapult**: A small ship-mounted catapult used to throw stones at enemy vessels. Loading and aiming a ship catapult requires a Utilize action, and firing it uses another. Multiple crew can operate the same siege weapon to perform these actions in the same round.

description.value: Some of the possible siege weapons are described here.

description.name: Movement (Sail and Rowing)
description.value: Use the Speed statistic provided with the vehicle. If you draw from another source, and the only Speed provided for a vehicle is in miles per hour, a handy approximation of the number of feet the ship moves per round is to take the value given for the vessel's miles per hour and multiply it by 10. This assumes the ship is being piloted. For example, a galley moves at 4 mph with average winds, or 40 ft. per round. If you are playing on a grid, round to the nearest multiple of 5 when counting squares. The Speed listed for longships includes its sail speed and its Rowing Speed.

description.name: Changing Direction
description.value: Sailing vessels don't quickly turn. A ship changing direction without completing a shipboard action moves the first half of its Speed in the direction it is facing and rotates 45° before moving the second half of its movement. For example, a turning galley would move 20 ft. in the direction it began the round and then another 20 feet at a 45° diagonal to its previous course.

description.name: Direction of Wind and Drifting
description.value: The direction of the wind is of critical importance to sailing a ship, determining if it can easily move in a straight line or is forced to tack back and forth. These rules simplify the importance of wind direction, assuming that the crew is tacking and making other appropriate adjustments to the sails. If a ship is not controlled, it drifts in the direction of the wind at the start of each of its turns: 5 feet for light wind, 10 feet for average wind, and 15 feet for strong wind. If the ship is being rowed, it generally ignores the effects of wind and drift, unless in storm conditions.

description.name: Turning Into the wind
description.value: The one direction ships never want to go is directly into the wind. A vessel that turns into the wind and tries to move in that direction has its Speed halved. If the ship's speed is greater than 0 feet while moving into the wind, the crew member at the helm must succeed on a DC 12 Strength (*Athletics*) or Wisdom (*Survival*) check to turn the ship. If the crew member fails to turn the ship, or the ship's Speed was reduced to 0 feet., it drifts in the direction of the wind and is stuck until the wind changes.

description.name: Wind Speed
description.value: Distance traveled assumes average wind speeds. Over the course of days, this is likely to be the case. During a combat round however, that doesn't have to be the case. If there is no wind, sailing ships don't move. If there are light winds, halve the ship's Speed, and if there are strong winds, double it. Longships also make use of rowers.
[See Wind's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#wind_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Sea Weather
description.value: Traveling by sea in a fantasy world means encountering strange weather in addition to the normal variations of wind and visibility. Use the Wind and Precipitation tables to determine weather conditions. Effects on movement assume the ship is powered by sails. If it is rowed or derives its power from some other source, an effect might not be relevant.
[See Precipitation's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#precipitation_northlandsworldbook)
[See Unusual Weather's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#unusual%20weather_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Naval Combat
description.value: A ship-to-ship battle can be a thrilling addition to your adventure. Without using the rules in this section, GMs can run ship encounters like any other combat. At the end of each round, all ships involved in the encounter can maneuver as the players or GM wishes. This is certainly the quickest method of handling naval combat.
For GMs and players who want more involved ship encounters, here is an optional set of rules to help create electrifying ship combats.

description.name: Crew Member Stat Blocks
description.value: The average sailor has the statistics of a __Bandit__ or __Pirate__. A quick stat block for an officer could be a __Pirate__ or a __Viking__ (see Chapter 8), while the captain might use a __Wolf Reaver Dwarf__ or __Pirate Captain__ stat block.

description.name: Initiative
description.value: Ships move and act last in Initiative, and their crews are assumed to be the ones performing the chosen action. Player characters and unique foes not concerned with running a ship roll Initiative as normal. However, determine Initiative between competing vessels each round.

To decide which ship acts first, determine which ship has the advantage of position by having the person at the helm of each ship make a Strength (*Athletics*) or Wisdom (*Survival*) check. The winner chooses whether to act first or delay. If the helm has no one assigned, that ship automatically fails the check.

description.name: Using Ship-Mounted Weapons
description.value: Unlike a standard siege weapon, large shipboard weapons require separate Utilize actions to load, aim, and fire. In a raiding party, it's assumed that sufficient crew members have been hired to operate all ship-mounted weapons. The Operate Ship Weapon action allows the crew to reload and aim the weapon, but it still requires another action to fire it. If an enemy is in the firing arc of a weapon, generally 90° from the direction it is mounted, the gunnery crew can attempt to fire on it.

description.name: Ship Damage
description.value: A ship taking damage in combat can suffer various effects. This damage can come as the result of weapon fire, spells, or impacts with physical objects. Consult the [Damage to the Ship](https://5e.tools/tables.html#damage%20to%20the%20ship_northlandsworldbook) table for the effects of damage to the hull.
[See Damage to the Ship's stats here](https://5e.tools/tables.html#damage%20to%20the%20ship_northlandsworldbook)

description.name: Targeting Crew and Casualties
description.value: Ship weapons typically aren't used against enemy sailors. The opposing vessel is a much easier target. However, sailors might be injured as collateral damage from an attack. When an attack scores a Critical Hit, in addition to rolling the damage dice twice, determine the location of the ship that was hit using the Disable Station shipboard action.

Roll a d6 to determine how many crew members in that area are Unconscious and dying. If a PC or NPC with medical skill or magical healing does not take action to save them, 75 percent of them die in 1d4 rounds. If a PC is in the area hit, they take half the damage dealt by the attack from flying shrapnel. If the PC succeeds on a Dexterity save with a DC equal to the enemy gunner's attack roll, they instead take no damage from shrapnel.

description.name: Actions During Ship Combat
description.value: During a naval engagement, the PCs can act independently from the ship with its crew, or they can work with them as determined by the players.

description.name: PCs During Combat
description.value: PCs can choose to act as they would in any other combat. Throwing __Fireball__ and raining down a volley of arrows remain effective tactics. Note however, that most engagements begin at (2d6 + 2) * 100 ((2d6 + 2) x 100) feet, so PC attacks are not generally in range when engagements commence. PCs can also use their turn to perform a shipboard action. A PC doing so must use the Ready action on their turn. Then, once the ship has moved at the end of the round, they can use their Reaction to do their readied shipboard action.

description.name: Ship and Crew During Combat
description.value: Ships and crew act at the end of the Initiative round. On its turn, a vehicle can move up to its Speed and use a shipboard action. The players should decide together what this ship action is going to be. PCs who delayed their actions on their turns can make additional shipboard actions. Unless noted otherwise, the same shipboard action can only be performed once per turn.

description.name: Shipboard Actions
description.value: There are a number of actions the crew of the ship (and potentially the PCs) can take in ship-to-ship combat.
[See All Stop's stats here](https://5e.tools/actions.html#all%20stop_northlandsworldbook)
